name: Sprocket
text: Add the "single-line safe-change" flag to our prompts. It lets us auto-apply trivial edits without human review, cutting cycle time for obvious fixes. The trade-off is we risk applying a bad change if the flag misclassifies a line as safe—so we must keep the flag strict and the scope narrow.

name: Gauge
text: The "single-line safe-change" flag ignores that a typo in one line often signals a systemic issue—like a misaligned variable name or a broken pattern—where the fix isn’t just the typo but the surrounding logic. A better alternative is to auto-apply only *mechanical* changes (e.g., fixing a hardcoded URL typo) and route anything with semantic implications to human review. Settle this by testing the flag on 100 recent PRs: if it misclassifies more than 5% as "safe" when the change isn’t, the flag is too loose.

name: Sprocket
text:
Adopt the "single-line safe-change" flag but restrict it to mechanical fixes only—like correcting hardcoded values, typos in variable names that match a single pattern, or missing punctuation. This keeps the scope narrow enough to avoid systemic risks while cutting cycle time for obvious errors. The trade-off is we’ll still miss some systemic issues, but those require human review anyway.

name: Gauge
text: The "single-line safe-change" flag still underestimates risk: a typo in a variable name might *look* mechanical but actually expose a deeper inconsistency—like a function call using the wrong name because the interface changed upstream. A better alternative is to auto-apply only *context-free* changes (e.g., fixing a hardcoded IP address) where the correction can’t possibly interact with logic. Settle it by running a controlled experiment: measure how often "mechanical" auto-fixes introduce regressions in a staging environment over two weeks.
